questions.q: What is the formal definition of an Architectural Design Competition (ADC) according to SPP Doc 208?
o: A government-mandated bidding process where the lowest bidder is automatically awarded the project.
A marketing event where architects bid for the lowest fee to secure a project commission.
A collaborative workshop where multiple architects work together on a single site plan.
A process where an Owner/Promoter invites architects to submit design proposals for a specific project, which are then evaluated by an independent jury.
questions.n: The ADC is a structured, competitive process where merit-based selection is handled by an impartial body of experts.

questions.q: What are the two main types of Architectural Design Competitions based on the eligibility of participants?
o: Local Competitions and International Competitions
Student Competitions and Professional Competitions
Open Competitions and Limited/Restricted Competitions
Public Competitions and Private Competitions
questions.n: Open competitions are available to all qualified professionals, while limited ones are restricted to invited or pre-qualified firms.

questions.q: What characterizes a 'Two-Stage Competition' according to professional standards?
o: A competition that requires a design stage followed by a separate construction stage.
A process where the first stage is for conceptual ideas (open), and selected competitors proceed to the second stage for detailed designs.
A competition where the architect must submit two different design options simultaneously.
A competition where you submit the design in the first year and the building permit in the second.
questions.n: This structure filters a high volume of ideas into a manageable short-list for more intensive development.

questions.q: In the context of an ADC, who is the 'Promoter'?
o: The person or organization (Owner) who initiates the competition and provides the prizes and commissions.
The marketing agency hired to advertise the competition.
The Professional Advisor who organizes the rules.
The head of the Jury who selects the winner.
questions.n: The promoter is the client who 'promotes' or launches the competition to find a design for their specific site.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of holding an Architectural Design Competition?
o: To get as many free ideas as possible from architects.
To find the best design solution and select the most capable architect through a fair and transparent process.
To bypass the standard fee scale for architectural services.
To create public controversy and media attention for a site.
questions.n: Competitions promote design excellence and ensure the client gets the best possible solution for their project.

questions.q: According to Doc 208, who must compose the majority of the Jury members?
o: Architects (Professional members)
Government officials and politicians
The Promoter's family members and employees
Celebrities and artists
questions.n: A technical and artistic majority of architects ensures the evaluation is grounded in professional competence and design quality.

questions.q: Can a member of the Jury or their business partner/employee enter the competition they are judging?
o: No. This is a strict conflict of interest and is prohibited.
Yes, provided they don't vote on their own entry.
Yes, but they can only win second place.
Only if the Promoter gives them special permission.
questions.n: To maintain impartiality, no judge or person associated with them may benefit from the competition entry pool.

questions.q: What is the role of the Professional Advisor in relation to the Jury?
o: To select the jury members based on their personal friendship.
To cast the deciding vote in case of a tie.
To assist in organizing the competition and ensuring rules are followed, without having a vote.
To act as the spokesperson for the winning architect.
questions.n: The advisor manages the logistics and compliance but leaves the design judgment entirely to the jury.

questions.q: Is the decision of the Jury binding on the Promoter?
o: Only if the winner is a Filipino architect.
Only if the project budget is over 100 million pesos.
Yes, unless the competition rules explicitly state otherwise.
No, the Promoter can choose any entry they like regardless of the Jury.
questions.n: The promoter agrees to abide by the expert panel's decision as a condition of launching the competition.

questions.q: What must the Jury produce at the end of the evaluation process to justify their selection?
o: A set of revisions for the winning architect to follow.
A brief press release with only the winner's name.
A bill for their professional services.
A Jury Report explaining the ranking of entries and reasons for the selection.
questions.n: This report provides transparency and educational value, explaining why the winning design best met the criteria.

questions.q: What is the 'Competition Brief' (or Program) in an ADC?
o: A document containing project requirements, site data, budget, constraints, and rules.
A short summary of the architect's biography.
A legal contract signed after the winner is selected.
A collection of photos showing what the client likes.
questions.n: The brief is the essential 'rulebook' and technical guide that all competitors must follow to ensure parity.

questions.q: What must be clearly defined in the scope regarding Prizes and Honoraria?
o: The exact amount of money to be awarded to the winner and any participation fees for shortlisted entries.
The percentage of the prize that goes to the jury.
That prizes will be determined only after the building is finished.
That the winner will receive 'exposure' instead of cash.
questions.n: Financial transparency ensures that architects can evaluate if the effort required is worth the potential reward.

questions.q: Is the winning architect automatically entitled to the Detailed Architectural and Engineering Design Services (DAEDS) contract?
o: Only if the owner likes the architect personally.
No, they only win the prize money.
Yes, the competition rules usually state that the winner will be awarded the commission for the project.
Only if they agree to work for half the standard fee.
questions.n: The commission is the ultimate 'first prize' in a professional competition.

questions.q: What happens to the Copyright of the losing entries in an ADC?
o: The Promoter owns all ideas submitted for future use.
The copyright is transferred to the IAPOA.
The designs become public domain.
The copyright remains with the respective Architect-Authors.
questions.n: The promoter only 'buys' the rights to use the winning design; all other intellectual property remains with the creators.

questions.q: What is the scope of the Technical Panel in a design competition?
o: A group of students who help with the exhibition.
The group that selects the winner.
The team that builds the 3D models for the competitors.
A group of experts who check entries for technical and budgetary compliance before the Jury evaluation.
questions.n: They ensure the jury only evaluates designs that are actually buildable and within the client's financial reach.

questions.q: Who is eligible to enter an Architectural Design Competition in the Philippines?
o: Only Registered and Licensed Architects (RLAs) in good standing with the PRC and IAPOA.
Civil Engineers who specialize in building design.
Only architects with more than 20 years of experience.
Anyone who can draw and has a passion for buildings.
questions.n: The law requires that architectural services be performed only by licensed professionals.

questions.q: Can a Foreign Architect enter a local architectural competition in the Philippines?
o: Only if the competition is held online.
Yes, they can enter independently if they have an international award.
No, competitions are strictly for citizens only.
Yes, but only in collaboration with a Filipino RLA and after obtaining an STP.
questions.n: Foreigners must follow RA 9266, which requires a local partner and a Special Temporary Permit from the PRC.

questions.q: Are Architecture Students allowed to enter professional ADCs under Doc 208?
o: No, unless it is specifically labeled as a 'Student Competition'.
Only if they are in their 5th year of study.
Yes, if they work for free.
Yes, as long as they have a high GPA.
questions.n: Professional competitions require a license because the winner will be awarded a legal contract for services.

questions.q: If a competition is 'Limited,' how is the eligibility of the participants determined?
o: Through a Pre-qualification process involving portfolios and experience reviews.
Based on who the Professional Advisor likes most.
By selecting the architects who live closest to the site.
Through a lottery system.
questions.n: The promoter filters for firms with the specific expertise needed for a complex or specialized project.

questions.q: Can an architect enter a competition if they were involved in writing the Competition Brief?
o: No. Anyone involved in the preparation or organization of the ADC is disqualified.
Only if the IAPOA grants a special waiver.
Yes, but they must use a different firm name.
Yes, because they understand the project best.
questions.n: To ensure absolute fairness, those who 'set the rules' cannot 'play the game'.

questions.q: What is the first formal step the Promoter must take to start an Architectural Design Competition?
o: Appoint a Professional Advisor to manage the process and coordinate with IAPOA.
Hire a contractor to start digging the site.
Announce the winner on social media.
Buy the furniture for the future building.
questions.n: The advisor ensures the entire process is set up according to professional standards from day one.

questions.q: Why must the ADC rules be approved by the IAPOA (UAP) before the competition is launched?
o: To ensure the rules are fair, ethical, and protect the professional rights of architects.
So the IAPOA can pick the winner in advance.
To ensure the building follows the National Building Code.
To make sure the IAPOA gets a cut of the prize money.
questions.n: The IAPOA acts as a watchdog to prevent promoters from using unfair terms or exploiting designers.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'Anonymity' rule during the submission and evaluation phase?
o: To ensure the Jury judges the design only, without knowing the architect's identity.
To keep the project a secret from the public.
To prevent the architect from being bothered by the media.
To allow the architect to submit work they didn't actually do.
questions.n: Anonymity prevents bias toward famous architects or personal friends of the jury.

questions.q: What is the 'Question and Answer' period in the ADC timeline?
o: An interview between the Jury and the finalists.
A period where the Promoter asks architects about their fees.
A public debate about the project's site.
A set time where competitors ask for clarifications, and answers are sent to all simultaneously.
questions.n: This ensures that no single architect has more information than the others.

questions.q: After the winner is announced, what is the final step usually held regarding the entries?
o: All losing entries are immediately shredded for security.
A secret meeting to discuss the winner's flaws.
A Public Exhibition of all entries to promote transparency and discourse.
The Promoter auctions off the losing designs to the highest bidder.
questions.n: Exhibitions celebrate the collective effort and allow the public to see the diversity of solutions.
